verdict.rationale: The proposition bundles two claims that the queried lexical data treat unequally. The claim that Christ's sacrifice is single and unrepeatable is strongly supported. Hebrews stacks 'once for all' (ephapax, G2178, Hebrews 7:27 and 9:12), 'one sacrifice' and 'one offering' (mian thysian and mia prosphora, G1520 with G2378 and G4376), 'forever' or 'continually' (eis to dienekes, G1336), the perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands) 'he has perfected' (teteleioken, G5048, tagged V-RAI-3S meaning perfect active indicative third person singular, Hebrews 10:14) and the aorist (a completed past action) 'he sat down' (ekathisen, Hebrews 10:12) to assert one finished offering, while Acts 1:9-11 fixes the same bodily Jesus ('this same Jesus,' houtos ho Iesous) in heaven until his return. But the narrower claim that 'is' (estin) in 'this is my body' (touto estin to soma mou, Matthew 26:26, Mark 14:22, Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24) is figurative rather than a substance change cannot be settled from the linking verb 'is' (the copula). The verb is G1510 in the bare V-PAI-3S form (present active indicative third person singular, an ongoing simple statement of fact), and the canon uses that very form both for identity and for representation (Matthew 13:38, Luke 8:11, John 15:1, and the imperfect tense, an ongoing or repeated past action, 'was' (en) at 1 Corinthians 10:4), with 1 Corinthians 11:25 calling the cup the new covenant in the same passage. The category 'transubstantiation' (a substance-change idea) names a metaphysic the vocabulary does not supply, so the words neither establish it nor strictly exclude a real presence. The predication is materially contested, so the bundled proposition is disputed even though its sacrifice-finality component is well grounded.

scripture.reasoning: At institution Jesus says 'this is my body' (touto estin to soma mou). The morphology in the store tags 'is' (estin) as G1510 in the form V-PAI-3S (present active indicative third person singular, the ordinary present linking verb 'is'), with the subject 'this' (touto) tagged G3778 D-NSN (a neuter demonstrative) agreeing with the neuter predicate 'the body' (to soma, G4983 N-NSN) rather than with the masculine 'bread' (arton, G0740) just handled. The linking verb 'is' (the copula) links subject and predicate but does not itself encode whether the predication is identity (this item is in substance my body) or representation (this stands for or conveys my body). Both senses are abundant for this exact verb form across the canon, so the surface grammar of 'is' (estin) is genuinely two valued and cannot by itself decide literal versus figurative predication, nor supply the substance-change category that the word 'transubstantiation' names.

Mark records the same words, 'having taken bread ... this is my body' (labon arton ... touto estin to soma mou), with the identical linking verb 'is' (estin, G1510, V-PAI-3S, present active indicative third person singular). The parallel across the Synoptic Gospels and Paul shows the predication is a fixed formula, but the repetition does not change the lexical openness of the linking verb 'is'. The same verb form carries identity in some contexts and representation in others, so the formula itself does not disambiguate.

Luke pairs 'this is my body' (touto estin to soma mou) with the command 'do this in remembrance of me' (touto poieite eis ten emen anamnesin). The noun 'remembrance' or 'memorial' (anamnesis, G0364) occurs only here and at 1 Corinthians 11:24-25 in the supper sayings (4 occurrences total). The memorial frame is lexically present in the institution itself, which is compatible with a representational reading of 'is' (estin), though it does not by itself exclude a real presence.

In the same supper account Paul writes 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood' (touto to poterion he kaine diatheke estin en to emo aimati), where 'is' (estin) is again G1510 V-PAI-3S (present active indicative third person singular). A cup cannot be a covenant by literal identity, so here the very same linking verb form must be representational or metonymic (one thing standing for another by close association). This is the clearest internal demonstration that the institution 'is' (estin) is two valued and is not, on its own, a claim of substantial change.

Immediately after the cup, Jesus calls it 'of this fruit of the vine' (ek toutou tou genematos tes ampelou), with 'vine' (ampelou) tagged G0288 in the store. After the words of institution the contents of the cup are still named by the ordinary term for the produce of the vine, which weighs against reading the institution words as asserting a completed change of substance, though it does not settle the presence question.

Paul writes 'for as often as you eat this bread' (hosakis gar ean esthiete ton arton touton), with 'bread' (arton, G0740) and the verb 'to eat' (esthio, G2068). After the consecration narrative the element is still called 'this bread' (ton arton touton), and verses 27-28 keep calling it 'bread' (arton). The continued lexical use of 'bread' for the consecrated element weighs against a completed substance change but does not by itself rule out a real presence under the form of bread.

Jesus says 'the one who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life' (ho trogon mou ten sarka kai pinon mou to haima echei zoen aionion). The verb 'to gnaw or chew' (trogo, G5176) is tagged here V-PAP-NSM (present active participle, nominative singular masculine, an ongoing action describing the one doing it), and is more graphically physical than 'to eat' (esthio). It occurs only 6 times in the New Testament, 4 of them in this discourse (verses 54, 56, 57, 58), so its sense cannot be triangulated from a wide spread. Its other two occurrences are ordinary table eating (Matthew 24:38, eating before the flood) and the betrayer eating bread in a Psalm citation (John 13:18), so 'to gnaw' (trogo) is not lexically restricted to literal cultic ingestion. Whether the intensified language demands corporeal eating or is heightened figure for believing appropriation is not decidable from morphology alone.

Within the same flesh-and-blood discourse Jesus says 'it is the Spirit who gives life, the flesh profits nothing, the words I have spoken to you are spirit and are life' (to pneuma estin to zoopoioun, he sarx ouk ophelei ouden, ta remata ha ego lelaleka humin pneuma estin kai zoe estin). The predicate 'is' (estin, G1510, V-PAI-3S, present active indicative third person singular) is applied to 'words' (remata), and 'the flesh profits nothing' (he sarx ouk ophelei ouden) steers the eating language toward a spiritual mode of appropriation rather than literal carnal consumption. This pulls against the realist 'to gnaw' (trogo) reading, and the discourse does not lexically rank the two.

Paul calls the cup 'participation in the blood of Christ' (koinonia tou aimatos tou Christou) and the bread 'participation in the body' (koinonia tou somatos), with 'participation' or 'sharing' (koinonia, G2842, 15 New Testament occurrences) tagged here and the predicate 'is' (estin, G1510) governing both. 'Participation' (koinonia) denotes participation or sharing, a relational category, not a substance-change verb. Lexically this supports a real participatory communion in the body and blood without requiring that the elements cease in substance to be bread and wine, but it also does not by itself exclude a substantial reading, so it tempers rather than settles the predication question.

The high priest no longer has 'daily necessity' (kath hemeran anagken) to offer sacrifices, because Christ did this 'once for all' (ephapax, G2178, tagged ADV meaning adverb), 'having offered himself' (heauton anenegkas, G0399, aorist, a completed past action). The adverb 'once for all' (ephapax) contrasts the single self-offering with the repeated Levitical 'sacrifices' (thysiai, G2378). This resists any reading in which the same sacrifice is re-presented or re-effected repeatedly.

Christ entered the holy place 'once for all' (ephapax, G2178) 'through his own blood' (dia tou idiou aimatos, G0129), having obtained 'eternal redemption' (aionian lytrosin). The 'once for all' (ephapax) plus the aorist (completed past action) 'he entered' (eiselthen) plus the result noun 'redemption' (lytrosin) marks a completed, non-repeated entry that secured a standing result, not an ongoing ritual repetition.

'This one' (houtos, G3778), 'having offered' (prosenegkas, G4374, aorist participle, a completed past action) 'one sacrifice for sins forever' (mian ... thysian, 'one sacrifice,' G1520 with G2378, and eis to dienekes 'continually' or 'forever,' G1336), 'sat down' (ekathisen, G2523, aorist, a completed past action). The numeral 'one' (mian) plus 'forever' (eis to dienekes) plus the aorist of sitting marks the offering as singular and finished, with the seated posture signaling completion rather than continuing priestly action.

By 'one offering' (mia prosphora, G1520 with G4376) 'he has perfected' those being sanctified 'forever' (eis to dienekes, G1336), where 'he has perfected' (teteleioken) is tagged G5048 V-RAI-3S (perfect active indicative third person singular, a completed action whose result still stands). The single instrumental 'one offering' (mia prosphora) plus the perfect 'he has perfected' (teteleioken) asserts a completed, enduring perfection from one offering, the strongest single statement against any repeated or re-presented sacrifice.

The men identify the ascended one as 'this same Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven' (houtos ho Iesous ho analemphtheis aph humon eis ton ouranon) and say he will come 'in the same way' (houtos hon tropon). The demonstrative 'this' (houtos, G3778) fixes the referent as the same bodily Jesus, 'to take up' (analambano, G0353) names the bodily taking up, and 'into heaven' (eis ton ouranon, G3772) locates that body in heaven, which bears on whether the same body is locally present in the elements on earth.

complicating_texts.resolution: The institution clause 'this is my body' (touto estin to soma mou) uses 'is' (estin), the bare linking verb G1510 in the form V-PAI-3S (present active indicative third person singular, an ongoing simple statement of fact). The store shows that exact form carrying both an identity sense and a representational sense. Parallel predications with the same form, 'the field is the world' (ho agros estin ho kosmos) and 'these are' (houtoi eisin, Matthew 13:38), 'the seed is the word' (ho sporos estin ho logos, Luke 8:11), and the imperfect tense (ongoing or repeated past action) 'and the rock was Christ' (he petra ... en ho Christos, 1 Corinthians 10:4), show the figurative predicate is well attested. Because the linking verb does not itself disambiguate, the lexical data cannot by themselves rule a substance change in or out from this verse. This is the core reason the bundled proposition is rated disputed rather than affirmed.

Paul warns that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup unworthily is 'guilty of the body and blood of the Lord' (enochos tou somatos kai tou aimatos tou kyriou), and verse 29 adds 'not discerning the body' (me diakrinon to soma). The strong relational and forensic language ties guilt to the body and blood and is often read as evidence of a real presence. Lexically, however, 'guilty' (enochos) plus a noun in the 'of-X' grammatical form (the genitive) denotes liability with respect to a person or thing offended and does not by itself assert that the elements are that body in substance, so the verse intensifies the presence question without resolving the predication.

Jesus says 'unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life' (ean me phagete ten sarka tou huiou tou anthropou kai piete autou to haima, ouk echete zoen). The aorist subjunctives (completed-action verbs in an 'if-then' clause) of 'to eat' (esthio, G2068, here 'you eat' (phagete) from G5315) and 'to drink' (pino) are concrete consumption verbs, and the realism appears to favor a literal eating reading, which is why it complicates the figurative case.

The verb shifts to 'the one who gnaws or chews' (ho trogon, G5176, to gnaw or chew), a present participle (ongoing-action form) recurring through verses 54-58. The store shows 'to gnaw' (trogo) occurs only 6 times in the New Testament, 4 here, plus ordinary table eating at Matthew 24:38 and the betrayer eating bread at John 13:18, so it is not lexically confined to literal cultic ingestion. Whether the intensified 'gnawing' (trogein) language demands corporeal eating or is heightened figure for believing appropriation is not decidable from morphology and the near hapax distribution (near-only-one-occurrence pattern) alone, and John 6:63 in the same discourse pulls toward the spiritual sense. This tension is left lexically unresolved, which is why the verdict is disputed.

variant_units_examined.note: Some witnesses read 'high priest' (archiereus) for 'priest' (hiereus) at the head of verse 11. The variant changes the priestly title but not the 'often' (pollakis) and 'daily' (kath hemeran) repetition contrast that carries the sacrifice-finality point.

Witnesses differ over the longer text of Luke 22:19b-20 ('which is given for you ... do this' (to hyper hymon didomenon ... touto poieite)). The presence or absence of the memorial command in Luke does not change the verdict, because 'this is my body' (touto estin to soma mou) and the 'remembrance' (anamnesis) command stand uncontested in 1 Corinthians 11:24-25 regardless.

Witnesses vary in word order and in the placement of 'I have spoken' (lelaleka), but the 'flesh' (sarx) and 'spirit' (pneuma) contrast and the predicate 'is' (estin) applied to 'words' (remata) are stable across readings.

variants.note: All cited texts are New Testament outside 3 John, so the critical edition of New Testament textual variants (the ECM apparatus) is not yet published for these books and they fall outside the ingested ECM window. Readings are taken from the standard critical editions in shadow mode. No examined variant shifts the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'is' (estin) in Matthew 26:26 as identity and the 'gnawing' (trogo) realism of John 6:54-58 plus 'true food' (alethes estin brosis) of John 6:55 and 'guilty of the body and blood' (enochos tou somatos kai tou aimatos) in 1 Corinthians 11:27 as pointing to a literal presence, so it rejects the claim that the elements remain bread and wine in substance. The linking verb 'to be' (G1510) and the eating verbs are lexically compatible with this reading, and the vocabulary does not exclude it.

Reads John 6:63 ('the flesh profits nothing, the words ... are spirit,' he sarx ouk ophelei ouden, ta remata ... pneuma estin) and the heavenly localization of the body in Acts 1:9-11 as steering toward a spiritual rather than substantial presence, with 'participation' (koinonia) at 1 Corinthians 10:16 naming relational participation, so the elements remain bread and wine while truly communicating Christ spiritually. The Hebrews 'once for all' (ephapax) cluster reinforces a non-repeated, non-re-presented offering. The linking verb 'is' is lexically open to this reading.

Reads 'is' (estin) as representational (this signifies my body) on the model of the same verb form in John 15:1, Matthew 13:38, Luke 8:11, and 1 Corinthians 10:4, reinforced by 1 Corinthians 11:25 where the cup is the new covenant and by the 'remembrance' (anamnesis) command. The elements signify but do not change in substance. The linking verb and the post-consecration terms 'bread' (arton) and 'fruit of the vine' (genema tes ampelou) are lexically open to this reading.

hermeneutics.notes: The Hebrews sacrifice-finality data ('once for all' (ephapax), 'one sacrifice' (mian thysian), 'forever' (eis to dienekes), the perfect tense (completed action whose result still stands) 'he has perfected' (teteleioken)) are stable across all three lenses and resist any repeated literal sacrifice, so that component of the proposition is firm. The narrower predication question (literal versus figurative 'is' (estin), the force of 'to gnaw' (trogo) in John 6) is where the lenses diverge, and the queried lexicon does not adjudicate between them because the same linking verb form carries both senses and 'to gnaw' (trogo) is a near hapax (a word that occurs only once or very rarely). Hence the lexical pattern supports part of the bundled proposition firmly while leaving the substance-change denial materially contested.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: In the Lord's Supper, what is the relationship between the bread and wine and Christ's body and blood, and does the institution language 'this is my body' (touto estin to soma mou) assert a change of substance, a signification, or a spiritual communication?
stem_audit.notes: The stem is framed as a denial of transubstantiation and pre-loads one disputed reading by asserting that the elements remain bread and wine in substance and by appending the parenthetical that under some accounts they communicate Christ spiritually. That parenthetical encodes a particular sacramental position rather than a neutral lexical question. The neutralized form poses the predication and presence question without presupposing the answer. The verdict was derived on the original stem and rendered disputed because the lexicon cannot settle the linking verb 'is' (the copula) and eating-verb predication, while the sacrifice-finality component is well supported. Verdict unchanged from the prior file (no VERDICT-CHANGED: marker applies); the direct store queries confirmed the 'is' (estin) morphology (G1510 V-PAI-3S, present active indicative third person singular, in Matthew 26:26 and in the figurative parallels), the near hapax (near-only-one-occurrence) distribution of 'to gnaw' (trogo), and the sacrifice-finality cluster, which all support keeping the disputed rating.

lay_summary: The question asks whether the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper stay bread and wine in substance, rather than changing into Christ's body and blood at the words of institution. Reading only the Greek and standard lexical tools, the evidence splits into two parts. One part is strong. Hebrews repeatedly uses 'once for all' (ephapax, Hebrews 7:27 and 9:12), then 'one sacrifice' (mian thysian), 'forever' (eis to dienekes), and the perfect-tense verb 'he has perfected' (teteleioken, a completed action whose result still stands, Hebrews 10:14), with 'he sat down' (Hebrews 10:12). Set against the daily and repeated Levitical offerings that could never take away sin, this describes one finished offering, not a sacrifice repeated or re-presented, and Acts 1:9-11 places the same bodily Jesus ('this same Jesus,' houtos ho Iesous) in heaven until his return. The other part is genuinely contested. The institution words 'this is my body' (touto estin to soma mou) turn on 'is' (estin), the simple verb 'to be.' In the store this verb is tagged the same way here as in 'the field is the world' (Matthew 13:38), 'the seed is the word' (Luke 8:11), 'I am the vine' (John 15:1), and 'the rock was Christ' (1 Corinthians 10:4), all of which are figurative. In the same supper account Paul even says the cup 'is' the new covenant, which cannot be a literal identity. So the verb by itself does not decide whether the bread is, in substance, the body, and the word 'transubstantiation' names a substance-change idea the vocabulary simply does not supply. John 6 sharpens the tension. Verses 53 to 58 use blunt eating verbs, including 'to gnaw' or 'chew' (trogo), which sounds literal, yet that rare word also covers ordinary eating elsewhere, and verse 63 in the same speech says 'the flesh profits nothing' and 'the words are spirit.' Because the verbs of being and eating support more than one defensible reading, and 'to gnaw' (trogo) is too rare to triangulate, the proposition is rated disputed. The sacrifice-finality claim is well grounded, but the narrower claim about how 'is' (estin) and the eating language work is not settled by the lexicon alone.
